titulo: The Olive Tree Is a Fiscal Policy
subtitulo: 1204, the crusader sack, and the four Venetian centuries that made Corfu another country (1204 – 1453)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look at

items.text: First, Corfu's two fortresses. The Old Fortress, on the promontory, is Byzantine at its core and Venetian in its present form; the New Fortress dates from the sixteenth century, after the siege of 1537. Look closely at the layout: angled bastions, moats, glacis. This is Italian Renaissance military architecture, essentially identical to that of Palmanova or Valletta, and it bears no relation whatsoever to Ottoman fortification. The island is built facing West, literally.

Second, the Liston, the arcade of the Esplanade, built under French occupation in the early nineteenth century in imitation of the rue de Rivoli. Its name comes from the "list" of noble families entitled to stroll beneath the arches. A public space that was, by definition, exclusionary, and that today is a terrace of cafés where anyone sits. Uses change; the layout remembers the social order that produced it. And beside it, the cricket ground, a British legacy from 1815–1864, with an active local league. Rarely do three empires read so quickly across a hundred meters.

Third, in Paxos, the olive groves and the old presses. The island has an even greater density of olive trees per unit of area, and its traditional economy was exactly that Venetian monoculture, with water scarcity as a permanent constraint. Ask about current production, about how many producers remain, about whether the oil is sold locally or exported in bulk without a brand. The answer — almost always, in bulk and unbranded — is a classic datum of dependency economics: the periphery produces, and someone else labels, bottles, and captures the margin. It is the same discussion as Peruvian coffee and cacao.

sections.heading: 1204: the crusade that attacked Christians
paragraphs: The Fourth Crusade set out from Venice in 1202 with Egypt as its declared destination and ended up sacking two Christian cities: Zara, on the Dalmatian coast, in 1202, at Venetian behest and against explicit papal prohibition; and Constantinople, between April 12 and 15, 1204. Three days of systematic plunder of the richest city in Christendom. The bronze horses that today stand at Saint Mark's in Venice came from there. So did the relics that filled the treasuries of half of Europe. Niketas Choniates, a Byzantine eyewitness, described prostitutes dancing on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and observed bitterly that the Saracens had been more merciful to Jerusalem.

The mechanism of the disaster deserves sociological attention because it was not a conspiracy but a chain of dependencies. The crusaders had contracted a Venetian fleet for thirty-three thousand men; twelve thousand showed up; they were left indebted for a sum they could not pay. The doge Enrico Dandolo, over ninety years old and blind, did not demand the money outright: he proposed services in compensation. First Zara. Then, exploiting a Byzantine dynastic dispute, Constantinople. The crusade ended up HELD HOSTAGE BY ITS OWN FINANCING: every step was rational given the debt, and the whole was a civilizational catastrophe. Any analysis of how an indebted country ends up executing policies it never chose recognizes the shape of this. Greece would experience it again, with accounting instruments in place of galleys, between 2010 and 2015.

The subsequent division of spoils was explicit: the Partitio Romaniae assigned Venice "a quarter and a half of a quarter" of the empire, that is, three-eighths, carefully chosen: ports, islands, straits. Venice did not want territory, it wanted NODES. Crete, Euboea, the Cyclades, and control of the Adriatic and the Ionian Sea. It is the first modern maritime empire in its logic: not to administer populations but to control routes, exactly like the commercial empires of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and just as contemporary capital controls ports and undersea cables without needing a flag.

sections.heading: A feudal Greece: Franks, Catalans, Florentines
paragraphs: Between 1204 and 1261, and in many regions until the fifteenth century, mainland Greece was governed by Western feudal lords. The Principality of Achaea organized the Peloponnese under its own feudal law, the Assizes of Romania. Athens was a duchy governed successively by Burgundians, by the Catalan Company — a band of Almogavar mercenaries who in 1311 annihilated the Frankish cavalry at Lake Copais and seized the duchy, ruling it for seventy years in Catalan and under the Aragonese crown — and then by the Florentine Acciaiuoli family. The Acropolis was, for two hundred and fifty years, a seigneurial castle with a Frankish tower that was only demolished in 1874, financed by Heinrich Schliemann, in another of those operations of cleansing away an uncomfortable past that we have already discussed.

Meanwhile, the empire fragmented into Greek successor states — Nicaea, Epirus, Trebizond — that competed with one another. Nicaea recovered Constantinople in 1261, but the restored empire was a husk: it had lost its fiscal base, its fleet, its trade, and much of its Anatolian territory, and it spent the next two centuries managing its own agony amid dynastic civil wars — that of 1341–1347 was especially ruinous — and tribute payments to neighboring powers.

One episode of that civil war deserves rescuing because it belies the image of an inert Byzantine world: between 1342 and 1350, in Thessaloniki, the movement of the ZEALOTS took power in the city, expelled the aristocracy, confiscated Church property, and governed autonomously for nearly eight years. It was a popular urban revolution in the middle of the fourteenth century, in the empire's second city, and it ended drowned in blood. The history of peripheries always contains these episodes of popular agency that narratives of decline erase, and the task of a sociological reading is precisely to rescue them without romanticizing them: the Zealots governed with factional violence and did not produce a stable order. But they existed.

sections.heading: Venetian Corfu: the island that was never Ottoman
paragraphs: Here begins the specific history of your destination, and it is worth underlining because it explains almost everything you will see. Corfu passed through Angevin hands, and in 1386 the island's own assembly of notables voluntarily submitted to Venice to escape Neapolitan instability. Venice governed Corfu, Paxos, and the other Ionian islands until 1797: FOUR HUNDRED AND ELEVEN YEARS. In that span, the island withstood the great Ottoman sieges of 1537, 1571, and 1716. It was never conquered by the Ottoman Empire.

The consequence is enormous and too little discussed. While mainland Greece spent four centuries under Ottoman administration — with the millet system, the Orthodox Church as intermediary, the poll tax on non-Muslims, and its own agrarian structure —, the Ionian islands lived under a Venetian colonial regime of the Western Mediterranean type: titled nobility inscribed in a GOLDEN BOOK, Italian as the language of administration, justice, and the elite, Catholicism as the religion of the rulers over an Orthodox majority whose clergy was hierarchically subordinated, and a seigneurial property regime. Corfu also had the first university of modern Greece — the Ionian Academy, 1824 — and the first opera house of southeastern Europe, the San Giacomo, in the eighteenth century.

This means that when the Greek state is built in the nineteenth century, the Ionian islands — only incorporated in 1864 — will contribute a Europeanized, Italian-speaking elite, with cultural habits and a class structure different from those of the mainland. Dionysios Solomos, author of the poem that would become the Greek national anthem, was a noble from Zakynthos who wrote Greek with difficulty and thought in Italian. The modern Greek nation was drafted in part by people formed outside the Ottoman experience. It is exactly the position of the enlightened Creole elites in Peruvian independence: formed within the colonizer's system, bearers of the national project, and structurally distant from the population in whose name they spoke.

sections.heading: The olive tree is a fiscal policy
paragraphs: Let us pause on the landscape, because it is the largest and most underrated historical document on the island. Corfu has, by the usual estimates, between three and four million olive trees, many of them with enormous, unpruned trunks, forming dense, shady woods that look nothing like the row-planted olive groves of Spain or Italy. That physiognomy is not natural: it is the result of a Venetian public policy. From the sixteenth century, and systematically in the seventeenth, the Republic offered premiums in gold sequins for every hundred olive trees planted, because it needed oil — for lighting, soap, and food — and preferred to produce it in its colony rather than buy it. Corfiot landowners planted massively, and, since labor was scarce and expensive, they adopted the practice of not pruning and of gathering the fallen olives from the ground with nets, which is still how it is done today.

What you are looking at, then, as you cross the island, is a COLONIAL MONOCULTURE fossilized in the landscape. And with it come all the known consequences of monoculture: dependence on a single product and a single buyer, vulnerability to price swings, relative abandonment of cereal production and therefore external food dependency, and a property structure concentrated in the families of the Golden Book with a peasantry working as tenants or sharecroppers. When, in the nineteenth century, Corfiot oil lost markets to Italian and Spanish oil, and when, in the twentieth, tourism offered higher returns, the olive groves were partly abandoned: what you see as melancholy beauty is also an archive of productive decline.

The Peruvian parallel is immediate and needs no forcing: guano between 1840 and 1879, Amazonian rubber between 1880 and 1912, the sugar and cotton of the coastal haciendas, and today mining. In every case, a product in demand from abroad reorganizes territory, property, and labor, generates an enriched intermediary elite, fails to link up with local production, and leaves behind a landscape and a social structure that outlive the economic cycle that created them. The difference with Corfu is aesthetic: there, the trace of extractivism is a forest of beautiful olive trees, and here it is open pits and tailings. The logic is the same. It is worth bearing in mind when someone tells you the island's landscape is "authentic": it is as authentic as any historical outcome, and its history is fiscal.

sections.heading: The Ottoman advance and Andean simultaneity
paragraphs: While Venice consolidated its maritime empire, the Ottomans advanced by land: Gallipoli in 1354, the first bridgehead in Europe; Kosovo in 1389; Nicopolis in 1396, where a Franco-Hungarian crusade was annihilated. Constantinople remained surrounded for fifty years, surviving as a tributary enclave. Tamerlane's invasion and the Ottoman defeat at Ankara in 1402 bought it half a century's reprieve; nothing more.

The global simultaneity of this period is among the most striking in history. The Mongols had destroyed Baghdad in 1258, closing the Islamic golden age. The Black Death, carried along Genoese trade routes from Caffa, killed between a third and half of the European population between 1347 and 1351, and struck the Byzantine and Ottoman worlds as well. China expelled the Mongols and founded the Ming dynasty in 1368; between 1405 and 1433 Zheng He's fleets reached East Africa with ships several times larger than European ones, after which the empire chose to suspend the expeditions. Portugal began, in 1415, its exploration of the African coast.

And in the Andes, exactly at this time, occurs what matters most for our mirror: under Pachacutec, beginning around 1438, Cusco launches the expansion that in three generations will produce Tahuantinsuyo, the largest state that ever existed in the Americas. That is: as Constantinople agonizes and falls, the Inca empire reaches its formative peak. Two worlds unaware of each other's existence undergo, in the same half-century, inverse processes — one is extinguished, the other culminates —, and both will be, in less than a century, absorbed into empires not their own. Comparative history is not useful for finding equivalences but for denaturalizing one's own timelines: nothing in the Byzantine decline was necessary, nothing in the Inca rise was guaranteed.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: 1204 as a living political argument
paragraphs: The sack of 1204 still works politically. Pope John Paul II expressed regret for it in 2001 before the archbishop of Athens, and in 2004, on the eight-hundredth anniversary, Bartholomew I received a formal expression of sorrow at the Vatican. That two religious leaders should negotiate the memory of an episode eight hundred years old indicates that the episode does work in the present: it is the founding stone of ORTHODOX ANTI-WESTERNISM, the historical proof that the West has betrayed Greece before and could do so again.

That sediment is not marginal. During the 2010–2015 crisis it fed both the anti-austerity left and the nationalist right, and it explains part of the diffuse sympathy toward Russia that certain sectors of Greek society maintain — on religious rather than ideological grounds — and which the war in Ukraine since 2022 has put under strain against Greece's membership in NATO and the European Union. In 2024–2026 that tension remains active and is visible in Greek public debate whenever military spending, sanctions, or the role of the Church is discussed.

The other resonance is material and lies in your own destination. Corfu's Venetian old town has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2007, and that status produces the characteristic conflict of inhabited urban heritage: rising housing costs, conversion of residences into short-term tourist rentals, displacement of the permanent population, and a cruise economy that unloads thousands of passengers a day with low per-capita spending and high pressure on water, waste, and public space. Several Mediterranean cities have begun to limit dockings and tax overnight stays; the debate is open in Greece and intensified after the record seasons of 2023 through 2025. You will see the phenomenon on the Esplanade and in the Campiello. And you will recognize it: it is the same discussion Cusco holds about its historic center, visitor caps, and who captures the visitor's rent.
